record.chaining: A CDXJ lookup on index.commoncrawl.org names the WARC file, offset and length of a stored capture and one byte-range GET on data.commoncrawl.org reads it, so a page Common Crawl captured is read from the crawl copy when a live fetch fails; for broad or large-scale URL filtering Common Crawl points callers to its URL Index (formerly the Columnar Index) through Amazon Athena or Apache Spark instead of the CDXJ API

limits.value: at most 1 request a second (HTTP level) on index.commoncrawl.org: the rate a Common Crawl engineer asked index callers to keep to on the Common Crawl user forum in April 2023

no concurrent requests from one IP address on the CDXJ API: callers are asked to sleep between calls, not to run multiple threads at once on the same IP and not to use proxy networks; an HTTP 503 answer means the acceptable request rate is exceeded
the CDXJ API on index.commoncrawl.org is heavily rate limited; an IP address that sends too many requests may be blocked, and a blocked IP address should wait 24 hours

record.provider: Common Crawl (the petabyte corpus — read side only)

free_tier.stated: Read-only corpus, free to download over HTTPS with no account; the October 2026 crawl alone is 2.16 billion pages, 109.20 TiB compressed. It holds Common Crawl's own crawls and takes no user data.

per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: the bucket stores no user objects; a read is a whole Common Crawl WARC file (958726164 bytes for one October 2026 file) or a byte range of one

retention.stated: one index per crawl, all still listed: collinfo.json names 129 crawl indexes, from CC-MAIN-2008-2009 to CC-MAIN-2026-43

egress.terms: Free and anonymous over HTTPS: 'The data is accessible via the https://data.commoncrawl.org/[...] URL scheme. There is no need to create an AWS account in order to access the data using this method.' S3 access (s3://commoncrawl) requires an authenticated AWS account. New: selected crawls are mirrored into a Hugging Face Storage Bucket with CDN pre-warming.

record.interface_detail: HTTPS GET with byte ranges on data.commoncrawl.org, no account; s3://commoncrawl through the S3 API; a Hugging Face Storage Bucket mirror of selected crawls with the same directory layout
record.tooling: cURL or wget against https://data.commoncrawl.org/, the AWS CLI against s3://commoncrawl/, the hf CLI against the Hugging Face Storage Bucket mirror, and Common Crawl's official downloader client cc-downloader
record.chaining: A read source, not a store: the crawl data is downloaded over HTTPS from data.commoncrawl.org, through the S3 API or from the Hugging Face Storage Bucket mirror into storage or compute held elsewhere, and its CDXJ index names the byte range of a single capture

limits.value: the CDXJ API on index.commoncrawl.org is heavily rate limited; an IP address that sends too many requests may be blocked, and a blocked IP address should wait 24 hours
under load the bucket answers 503 Slow Down to every caller; whole-file downloads recover when retried no more than once per second, index lookups and byte-range reads of single captures do not

record.limits_note: An unsigned GET to the S3 endpoint commoncrawl.s3.amazonaws.com answered 403 on 2026-10-30 and again on 2026-11-03, while HTTPS on data.commoncrawl.org and the Hugging Face bucket mirror served the same WARC file list with no account. The Get Started page still shows --no-sign-request commands in a second AWS CLI section.

record.notes: Fails the storage quota filter: the bucket holds only Common Crawl's own crawls of the web and takes no user data, so it offers no allowance a user can write to. One offer with crawler-scraper/commoncrawl, the same corpus judged as a crawl archive, which keeps qualifies-with-caveat as a read source.

dead_end.why: Not a hosting service: ~300 billion web pages across ~100+ monthly crawls, multi-petabyte, free to READ and free to re-host yourself. There is NO path to host your own data with Common Crawl — confirmed, it publishes its own crawls only.

record.binding_note: the CDXJ index on index.commoncrawl.org is heavily rate limited and can block a caller's IP address, which bounds lookups of single captures; a whole-file download, once it starts, runs without further rate checks
